title: Rehras at dusk
hookLine: the evening prayer, said as the day's work ends

cards: There's a moment at the end of a workday. You shut the laptop, or clock out, or take off your boots at the door. The bag hits the floor.

For a second you're between things: the day's not quite over, the evening hasn't started. It's easy to fill that second with the phone, the news, the next chore. In Sikh practice, that moment belongs to something else.
As the sun goes down, someone lights a lamp, or just sits, and the evening prayer begins.

teach.b: Rehras Sahib is the Sikh evening bani, said around sunset as the day's work ends.
It's a collection, not a single hymn: hymns of the Gurus from the Guru Granth Sahib, then Chaupai, part of Anand Sahib and a few closing verses. So you've met some of it this week.
It opens with So Dar, that door, a version of a passage from Japji, and it asks a huge, open question.

teach.h: SO DAR — WHAT IS THAT DOOR?
teach.b: In paraphrase: what is that door, and what is that home, where you sit and care for all? Then it answers with music. Countless instruments play there; countless singers in countless ragas sing your praise.
Wind, water and fire sing; the continents and the worlds sing.
At the end of a long day, when your world has shrunk to your inbox and your sore feet, Rehras opens the window as wide as it goes. And the name? Readers explain it more than one way.
Some connect it to a word for supplication, a humble petition.

Others hear rah, a road, and read it as provisions for the journey. Both fit: a pause for the traveler where the day's road runs out. The hymns return the day to the hukam, the Divine Order that sustains it all.
Said at sunset, they can be heard as handing the day back: what you did, what was done to you, set down inside something larger before the night.

how: Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib at sunset, at home or in the gurdwara, as the evening part of Nitnem; it opens with So Dar and includes Chaupai and part of Anand Sahib.

o: a Sikh prayer for rest days and holidays

games.q: the day's work is over and you're exhausted. what does Rehras open with?
o: a list of the day's mistakes.

games.why: So Dar: what is that door, that home, where you sit and care for all? then the whole creation is heard singing.

practice: Sit down as if it were dusk, hands resting in your lap, and bring up three things from today or yesterday: one you did, one that happened to you, one still unfinished.
As you breathe out, picture setting each one down on a table beside you, not solving it, just putting it down. If you pray, you can hand them over.

carryVoice: Your line: put the day down. At dusk, the window opens wide. That's day one hundred thirty-four.
